extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, litigants, and data controllers handling cross-border U.S. civil discovery and data-protection conflicts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for managing preservation, disclosure, and production of data that is subject to foreign Data Protection Laws in U.S. civil litigation, including principles for courts, parties, and data controllers to minimize conflicts of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of preservation / preservation obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary precondition for effective discovery is that the information has been preserved, giving rise to a duty of preservation. The preservation obligation makes it unlawful for any party to destroy, hide, or render unusable information that is relevant to a claim or defense. The preservation obligation arises when a party first learns of the litigation or should have reasonably anticipated it—not merely when litigation is 'possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to compel a party to maintain and safeguard information likely to be requested through discovery even if harmful to the party. Failing to preserve documents and ESI may be remedied or punished by the court (e.g., additional discovery, monetary sanctions, or dispositive judgment). The duty does not require preservation of every possible piece of data; reasonable steps to preserve suffice (Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(e) intent to curtail excessive preservation). See cases such as Rimkus, Zubulake, Victor Stanley, and Apple v. Samsung for scope examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession, custody, or control
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a responding party has 'possession, custody, or control' of information is the touchstone for preservation and production obligations under U.S. law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis is intensely fact-based and courts apply divergent tests (e.g., 9th Circuit's 'legal right' test vs. 'practical ability to obtain' test). A court must determine whether a party has sufficient control over an agent, corporate affiliate, or other entity holding the data to require production. See Genentech v. Univ. of Pa., In re Kaprun, S2 Automation v. Micron, and The Sedona Conference commentary for approaches and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onset of preservation duty — 'reasonable anticipation' trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to preserve relevant information arises when litigation is 'reasonably anticipated' — i.e., when an organization is on notice of a credible probability that it will become involved in litigation, seriously contemplates initiating litigation, or takes specific actions to commence litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations often must be made early; Data Controllers may need to decide applicability of Data Protection Laws and what data is protected before full facts are known. See The Sedona Conference Commentary on Legal Holds and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' authority to order extraterritorial production
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. courts have the authority to order production of information located outside the U.S. even if disclosure is restricted or prohibited by the law of another country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before exercising that authority courts weigh factors pursuant to U.S. Supreme Court guidance (Aérospatiale) and other considerations; the possibility of civil, administrative, or criminal sanctions in the foreign jurisdiction may not alone prevent a U.S. court from ordering production. Courts perform a comity/balancing analysis and consider proportionality and alternative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage approach for harmonization (TSC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where discovery and Data Protection Laws may conflict, parties should follow a three-stage approach: (1) stipulation or court order extending special protections to data covered by Data Protection Laws; (2) a scheduling order that phases discovery to permit time to implement data-protection processes and determine availability of similar information from non-protected sources; and (3) implementation of a legitimization plan by the parties to maximize simultaneous compliance with foreign data protection law and U.S. discovery obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is rooted in cooperation among lawyers, parties, judges, and data protection authorities and aims to avoid or minimize conflicts. The Sedona Conference Cooperation Proclamation endorses collaborative behavior to reduce costs and delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 1 — due respect for Data Protection Laws / international comity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and parties should demonstrate due respect to the Data Protection Laws of any foreign sovereign and the interests of any person who is subject to or benefits from such laws when data is subject to preservation, disclosure, or discovery in a U.S. proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comity requires balancing domestic and foreign interests (Aérospatiale). This 'due respect' standard does not mean automatic deference—comity has limits when foreign acts are fundamentally prejudicial to domestic forum policies. Parties must not invoke Data Protection Laws for improper purposes or to delay discovery absent a good-faith belief in a conflict (see Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) and related case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 2 — good faith and reasonableness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Where full compliance with both Data Protection Laws and U.S. preservation, disclosure, and discovery obligations presents a conflict, a party’s conduct should be judged by courts or data protection authorities under standards of good faith and reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties and Data Controllers should make good-faith, reasonable efforts to reconcile obligations; courts and authorities should evaluate actions based on the efforts made under circumstances existing at the time. 'Good faith' is often treated as a subjective standard and 'reasonableness' as an objective one. Proportionality and context are central; parties should attempt to meet and confer and pursue reasonable steps (e.g., seeking waivers from blocking statutes where appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 3 — limit preservation/discovery to what is relevant and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Preservation, disclosure, and discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense in order to minimize conflicts of law and impact on the Data Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Principle emphasizes heightened scrutiny for Protected Data: parties, Data Controllers, and courts should focus on information 'relevant and necessary' to claims/defenses and apply proportionality. If equivalent information is available from non-protected sources, seek to use those sources. Where disclosure is required (e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A)(ii)), take measures to comply with Data Protection Laws (confidentiality orders, stipulations). Do not produce Protected Data outside the scope of required disclosure merely for strategic advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Data Controller
rubrics_metrics.description: "Data Controller" is the natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or any other body which alone or jointly with others determines the purposes and means for the processing and transfer of Protected Data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under GDPR a Data Processor can in some circumstances be subject to similar accountability as a Controller; the Principles use these terms intentionally to align with common data-protection terminology but remain agnostic as to national interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Data Protection Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: "Data Protection Laws" include any law or regulation that restricts the usage or disclosure of data, requires safeguarding data, or imposes obligations in the event of compromises to the security or confidentiality of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to apply broadly irrespective of national origin, including privacy regulations, blocking statutes, trade secret protections, and other statutory/regulatory regimes that could conflict with U.S. discovery obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Data Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "Data Subject" is any person or entity whose Protected Data is or may be processed, transferred, or disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles emphasize minimizing impact on Data Subjects when balancing discovery and Data Protection Laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Processing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Processing" includes any operation, activity, use, or application performed upon Protected Data by automatic or other means, such as collection, recording, storage, alteration, retrieval, disclosure, or transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition is intended to cover actions from low-level data handling through information assembly in any media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Protected Data
rubrics_metrics.description: "Protected Data" is any data irrespective of its form (e.g., paper, ESI, images, etc.) that is subject to Data Protection Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'data' is used to convey coverage of data at any level of abstraction and any recording medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — U.S. Litigation (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: "U.S. Litigation" includes civil proceedings requiring the discovery of relevant information whether in federal, state, or other U.S. fora and excludes criminal proceedings or government investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Principles apply to civil discovery contexts; separate guidance may apply for internal or government investigations (see related Sedona materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality in cross-border discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering cross-border discovery and conflicts with foreign Data Protection Laws, courts and parties should apply proportionality—balancing competing factors to achieve a practical compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportionality factors include importance to the litigation, specificity of request, availability of alternative means, importance of issues at stake, amount in controversy, parties’ relative access to information, parties’ resources, and whether the burden or expense outweighs likely benefit. Federal Rules (e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1), 26(b)(2)(C)(iii)) embody proportionality and require limiting discovery that is not relevant or proportionate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation and meet-and-confer obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperation among adversaries, judges, and data protection authorities is a central tenet to minimize conflicts: parties are required to meet and confer in good faith to agree on discovery plans and to attempt to resolve data-protection conflicts before court intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sedona Conference Cooperation Proclamation and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) support collaborative behavior to reduce costs and delays. Failure to engage cooperatively or efforts to advance Data Protection Laws for improper purposes may be viewed as bad faith.
